passages.title: The desired visit includes receiving encouragement
passages.summary: Paul opens a letter to the believers in Rome. He calls himself an apostle set apart for God’s good news about his Son. He thanks God that their faith is known in all the world. He has often planned to visit and has been prevented. He says he is not ashamed of the good news. It is God’s power to save the Jew first and also the Greek. God’s wrath, he says, falls on those who trade his glory for images. God gives them up to their desires, and Paul lists the wrongs that follow.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show intended destinations named in the letter. They do not prove completed journeys.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches courage in sharing the gospel. Why does Paul explain his visit through mutual encouragement?

contextNote.title: The desired visit includes receiving encouragement
contextNote.text: Paul has wanted to visit Rome and has been prevented (verse 13). Verse 11 says he wants to give them a spiritual gift. Verse 12 corrects that at once with “that is.” He will be encouraged too, by their faith and his together. The gift runs both ways. Verse 15 keeps his aim plain: to tell the good news in Rome.

passages.title: Judging others does not remove the judge from judgment
passages.summary: Paul turns to a person who judges others. He says the judge does the same things and will not escape God’s judgment. God’s kindness is meant to lead to repentance. God will repay each one according to works, Jew first and also Greek. There is no partiality with God. Gentiles without the law sometimes do what the law requires. Paul then questions a Jewish teacher of the law who breaks it. He says true circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show intended destinations named in the letter. They do not prove completed journeys.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects inward commitment with conduct. Why does judging another person fail to establish the judge’s innocence?

contextNote.title: Judging others does not remove the judge from judgment
contextNote.text: Chapter 1 ended with a list of wrongs that a reader could condemn. Verse 1 begins with “therefore” and turns on that reader. The one who judges does the same things. So the verdict he gives on others falls on himself. Verse 3 asks if he thinks he will escape. Verse 4 names what he has missed: God’s kindness was meant to bring repentance. Verse 11 gives the rule under all of it: God has no favorites.

passages.title: One God prevents either people from owning the gift
passages.summary: Paul asks what advantage the Jew has and answers that it is great. They were entrusted with God’s words. Still he says Jews and Greeks are all under sin. He quotes a chain of Scriptures: no one is righteous. The law stops every mouth and gives knowledge of sin. Now God’s righteousness comes apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ. All have sinned, and all are justified freely by grace. Boasting is shut out, and faith upholds the law.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show intended destinations named in the letter. They do not prove completed journeys.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches grace as God’s gift rather than earned salvation. How does one God connect the two peoples in Paul’s argument?

contextNote.title: One God prevents either people from owning the gift
contextNote.text: Verse 27 asks where boasting is, and answers that it is shut out. Verse 28 says a person is justified by faith, apart from works of law. Verse 29 tests that with a question about God. If the law were the way, God would be the God of Jews only. Verse 30 answers that there is one God. He justifies the circumcised and the uncircumcised by the same faith. Verse 31 adds that this does not cancel the law.

passages.title: Abraham's trust comes before the sign
passages.summary: Paul takes Abraham as his example. Scripture says Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. A worker’s pay is owed, but this was counted as a gift. David also calls blessed the one whose sin the Lord does not count. Paul asks when Abraham was counted righteous. It was before he was circumcised. The promise came through faith, so it holds for all his offspring. Abraham trusted God for a son when he was about a hundred years old.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show intended destinations named in the letter. They do not prove completed journeys.

lds.text: Why does the timing of Abraham’s circumcision matter?

contextNote.title: Abraham's trust comes before the sign
contextNote.text: Verse 9 asks whether the blessing is only for the circumcised. Verse 10 answers with the order of events in Abraham’s life. He was counted righteous first and circumcised later. Verse 11 then calls circumcision a sign and seal of the faith he already had. That order makes him father of two groups. He is father of all who believe without circumcision (verse 11). He is also father of the circumcised who walk in that faith (verse 12).

passages.title: The gift arrives while its recipients remain enemies
passages.summary: Paul says those justified by faith have peace with God. They rejoice in hope and even in sufferings. Suffering produces perseverance, character, and hope. Christ died for the ungodly while they were still weak. Those once enemies are reconciled through his death. Paul then compares Adam and Christ. Through one man sin and death came to all. Through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show intended destinations named in the letter. They do not prove completed journeys.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects grace with changed conduct. Why does Paul stress that Christ died while the recipients remained sinners?

contextNote.title: The gift arrives while its recipients remain enemies
contextNote.text: Verse 5 says hope does not disappoint, because God’s love is poured out. Verses 6–8 show how that love is known. Verse 7 sets the human limit: one will hardly die even for a righteous person. Verse 8 puts Christ’s death outside that limit. He died for us “while we were yet sinners.” The timing is the proof. Verse 10 argues from it: enemies were reconciled, so the reconciled will be saved.

passages.title: Baptism joins death with a changed way of living
passages.summary: Paul asks if believers should keep sinning so that grace may grow. He answers that it must never be. Those baptized into Christ were baptized into his death. The old self was crucified with him, and the dead are freed from sin. They are to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God. Paul asks again if freedom from law permits sin. He says a person is a servant of what he obeys. The wages of sin is death, but God’s free gift is eternal life.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show intended destinations named in the letter. They do not prove completed journeys.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches that grace calls believers toward changed conduct. How does the contrast between wages and gift shape the closing verse?

contextNote.title: Baptism joins death with a changed way of living
contextNote.text: Verse 1 raises an objection to chapter 5. If grace grows where sin grows, why not sin more? Verse 2 says those who died to sin cannot go on living in it. Verse 4 explains that death by what baptism does. The baptized are buried with Christ into his death. The purpose follows: as Christ was raised, they walk in new life. Verse 11 tells them to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God.

passages.title: The law is good even when sin uses its command
passages.summary: Paul says the law binds a person only while he lives. A wife is free to marry again when her husband dies. So believers died to the law through Christ’s body and belong to another. Paul asks if the law is sin and denies it. He would not have known coveting without the command not to covet. Sin used the command and brought death. He describes wanting the good and doing the evil he hates. He cries out for rescue and thanks God through Jesus Christ.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show intended destinations named in the letter. They do not prove completed journeys.

lds.text: Why does Paul distinguish the command from sin’s use of it?

contextNote.title: The law is good even when sin uses its command
contextNote.text: Verse 5 said sinful passions worked “through the law.” That could sound as if the law itself is sin (verse 7). Paul separates the two. The law showed him what coveting is (verse 7). Sin took the command as its opening and deceived him (verses 8 and 11). Verse 12 therefore clears the law: it is holy, righteous, and good. Verse 13 places the blame: sin worked death through a good thing.

passages.title: The Spirit helps within weakness rather than removing every groan
passages.summary: Paul says there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. God sent his Son to do what the law could not. Those led by God’s Spirit are God’s children and call him Abba, Father. They are heirs with Christ if they suffer with him. Creation groans and waits to be set free from decay. Believers groan too and wait in hope. The Spirit helps them pray. Paul says nothing can separate them from God’s love in Christ.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show intended destinations named in the letter. They do not prove completed journeys.

lds.text: The selected lesson teaches becoming like Heavenly Father through Jesus Christ. This is Church teaching. How does the Spirit help when believers cannot supply fitting words?

contextNote.title: The Spirit helps within weakness rather than removing every groan
contextNote.text: Verses 22–23 describe two groans: creation’s and the believers’. Both wait for something not yet seen (verses 24–25). Verse 26 adds a third groan, and it is the Spirit’s. The weakness it names is exact: we do not know how to pray. The Spirit pleads for us with groans that cannot be spoken. Verse 27 says God, who searches hearts, knows the Spirit’s mind.

passages.title: The argument begins with grief and Israel's received gifts
passages.summary: Paul says he has great sorrow for his own people, the Israelites. He lists their gifts, and says Christ came from them by descent. He says God’s word has not failed. Not all descended from Israel are Israel, as Isaac and Jacob show. God told Moses he has mercy on whom he will. Paul answers an objector with the potter and the clay. He quotes Hosea and Isaiah on a people called and a remnant saved. Israel pursued righteousness by works and stumbled over the stone.

lds.text: Why does Paul begin with Israel’s gifts and his own grief?

contextNote.title: The argument begins with grief and Israel's received gifts
contextNote.text: Chapter 8 ended with nothing able to separate believers from God’s love. That raises a question about Israel, and Paul starts with grief (verse 2). He would accept being cut off for their sake (verse 3). Verse 4 then lists what is theirs, in the present tense. Adoption, glory, covenants, the law, the service, and the promises are theirs. Verse 5 adds the fathers and the Christ. Only after that does verse 6 say God’s word has not failed.

passages.title: Calling depends on hearing, and hearing depends on sent speakers
passages.summary: Paul says his prayer for Israel is that they be saved. They have zeal for God but not according to knowledge. He says Christ is the fulfillment of the law for everyone who believes. The word is near, in the mouth and in the heart. Whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised him will be saved. There is no distinction between Jew and Greek. Paul asks how people can call on one they have not heard. He quotes Isaiah: not all obeyed, yet God held out his hands all day.
passages.uncertainty: Selected markers show intended destinations named in the letter. They do not prove completed journeys.

lds.text: The selected lesson connects hearing with growing faith. What must happen before another person can hear and call?

contextNote.title: Calling depends on hearing, and hearing depends on sent speakers
contextNote.text: Verse 13 promises that whoever calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. Verse 14 asks what must come before that call. The questions step backward: calling needs belief, belief needs hearing, hearing needs a speaker. Verse 15 adds the last step: the speaker must be sent. Verse 17 sums it up: faith comes by hearing. Then verse 18 asks if Israel has heard, and answers yes. Verse 21 ends with God’s hands held out all day to Israel.

passages.title: The added branches must not boast against their supporting root
passages.summary: Paul asks if God has rejected his people and says no. He is an Israelite himself, and a remnant remains as in Elijah’s day. Israel’s stumble has brought salvation to the Gentiles. Paul compares Israel to an olive tree. Some branches were broken off, and wild branches were grafted in. He warns the wild branches not to boast, for they can be cut off. God is able to graft the natural branches in again. Paul says all Israel will be saved and ends with praise.

lds.text: Why must the added branches refuse to boast over the root?

contextNote.title: The added branches must not boast against their supporting root
contextNote.text: Verse 13 says Paul now speaks to Gentiles. Verse 17 gives their place: wild olive branches grafted in among the others. They share the root; they did not grow it. Verse 18 forbids boasting over the broken branches and gives the reason. The root holds them up, and they do not hold up the root. Verse 20 says they stand only by faith and should fear. Verse 23 adds that God can graft the others in again.

passages.title: Peace requires effort without pretending one person controls every response
passages.summary: Paul urges the believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice. They are not to be shaped by this world but changed by a renewed mind. No one should think too highly of himself. They are one body with many members and different gifts. Paul lists the gifts and then short commands about love. Bless those who persecute you. Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. Leave revenge to God, feed a hungry enemy, and overcome evil with good.

lds.text: How do the peace command’s limits affect personal responsibility?

contextNote.title: Peace requires effort without pretending one person controls every response
contextNote.text: Verse 17 forbids paying back evil with evil. Verse 18 gives the positive side and adds two limits. “If it is possible” admits that peace may not be reached. “As much as it is up to you” marks the part a person controls. The other person’s answer is not in that part. Verse 19 names what is given up: revenge belongs to God. Verse 20 names what remains to do: give an enemy food and drink.

passages.title: Love explains the commands through the harm they prevent
passages.summary: Paul tells every person to be subject to the governing authorities. He says they are appointed by God and carry the sword against wrongdoing. Believers should pay taxes, customs, respect, and honor where owed. They should owe nothing except love for one another. Love of neighbor sums up the commands against adultery, murder, theft, and coveting. Paul says the night is nearly over and the day is near. They should put away deeds of darkness. They should put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

events.title: The desired visit includes receiving encouragement
events.summary: Paul opens a letter to the believers in Rome. He calls himself an apostle set apart for God’s good news about his Son. He thanks God that their faith is known in all the world. He has often planned to visit and has been prevented. He says he is not ashamed of the good news. It is God’s power to save the Jew first and also the Greek. God’s wrath, he says, falls on those who trade his glory for images. God gives them up to their desires, and Paul lists the wrongs that follow.
events.detail: Paul has wanted to visit Rome and has been prevented (verse 13). Verse 11 says he wants to give them a spiritual gift. Verse 12 corrects that at once with “that is.” He will be encouraged too, by their faith and his together. The gift runs both ways. Verse 15 keeps his aim plain: to tell the good news in Rome.

events.title: Judging others does not remove the judge from judgment
events.summary: Paul turns to a person who judges others. He says the judge does the same things and will not escape God’s judgment. God’s kindness is meant to lead to repentance. God will repay each one according to works, Jew first and also Greek. There is no partiality with God. Gentiles without the law sometimes do what the law requires. Paul then questions a Jewish teacher of the law who breaks it. He says true circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit.
events.detail: Chapter 1 ended with a list of wrongs that a reader could condemn. Verse 1 begins with “therefore” and turns on that reader. The one who judges does the same things. So the verdict he gives on others falls on himself. Verse 3 asks if he thinks he will escape. Verse 4 names what he has missed: God’s kindness was meant to bring repentance. Verse 11 gives the rule under all of it: God has no favorites.

events.summary: Paul asks what advantage the Jew has and answers that it is great. They were entrusted with God’s words. Still he says Jews and Greeks are all under sin. He quotes a chain of Scriptures: no one is righteous. The law stops every mouth and gives knowledge of sin. Now God’s righteousness comes apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ. All have sinned, and all are justified freely by grace. Boasting is shut out, and faith upholds the law.

If the law were the way, God would be the God of Jews only. Verse 30 answers that there is one God. He justifies the circumcised and the uncircumcised by the same faith. Verse 31 adds that this does not cancel the law.

events.title: Abraham's trust comes before the sign
events.summary: Paul takes Abraham as his example. Scripture says Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. A worker’s pay is owed, but this was counted as a gift. David also calls blessed the one whose sin the Lord does not count. Paul asks when Abraham was counted righteous. It was before he was circumcised. The promise came through faith, so it holds for all his offspring. Abraham trusted God for a son when he was about a hundred years old.

Verse 11 then calls circumcision a sign and seal of the faith he already had. That order makes him father of two groups. He is father of all who believe without circumcision (verse 11). He is also father of the circumcised who walk in that faith (verse 12).

events.summary: Paul says those justified by faith have peace with God. They rejoice in hope and even in sufferings. Suffering produces perseverance, character, and hope. Christ died for the ungodly while they were still weak. Those once enemies are reconciled through his death. Paul then compares Adam and Christ. Through one man sin and death came to all. Through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous.

Verse 7 sets the human limit: one will hardly die even for a righteous person. Verse 8 puts Christ’s death outside that limit. He died for us “while we were yet sinners.” The timing is the proof. Verse 10 argues from it: enemies were reconciled, so the reconciled will be saved.

events.title: Baptism joins death with a changed way of living
events.summary: Paul asks if believers should keep sinning so that grace may grow. He answers that it must never be. Those baptized into Christ were baptized into his death. The old self was crucified with him, and the dead are freed from sin. They are to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God. Paul asks again if freedom from law permits sin. He says a person is a servant of what he obeys. The wages of sin is death, but God’s free gift is eternal life.

Verse 4 explains that death by what baptism does. The baptized are buried with Christ into his death. The purpose follows: as Christ was raised, they walk in new life. Verse 11 tells them to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God.

events.title: The law is good even when sin uses its command
events.summary: Paul says the law binds a person only while he lives. A wife is free to marry again when her husband dies. So believers died to the law through Christ’s body and belong to another. Paul asks if the law is sin and denies it. He would not have known coveting without the command not to covet. Sin used the command and brought death. He describes wanting the good and doing the evil he hates. He cries out for rescue and thanks God through Jesus Christ.
events.detail: Verse 5 said sinful passions worked “through the law.” That could sound as if the law itself is sin (verse 7). Paul separates the two. The law showed him what coveting is (verse 7). Sin took the command as its opening and deceived him (verses 8 and 11). Verse 12 therefore clears the law: it is holy, righteous, and good. Verse 13 places the blame: sin worked death through a good thing.

events.title: Calling depends on hearing, and hearing depends on sent speakers
events.summary: Paul says his prayer for Israel is that they be saved. They have zeal for God but not according to knowledge. He says Christ is the fulfillment of the law for everyone who believes. The word is near, in the mouth and in the heart. Whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised him will be saved. There is no distinction between Jew and Greek. Paul asks how people can call on one they have not heard. He quotes Isaiah: not all obeyed, yet God held out his hands all day.
events.detail: Verse 13 promises that whoever calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. Verse 14 asks what must come before that call. The questions step backward: calling needs belief, belief needs hearing, hearing needs a speaker. Verse 15 adds the last step: the speaker must be sent. Verse 17 sums it up: faith comes by hearing. Then verse 18 asks if Israel has heard, and answers yes. Verse 21 ends with God’s hands held out all day to Israel.

events.summary: Paul asks if God has rejected his people and says no. He is an Israelite himself, and a remnant remains as in Elijah’s day. Israel’s stumble has brought salvation to the Gentiles. Paul compares Israel to an olive tree. Some branches were broken off, and wild branches were grafted in. He warns the wild branches not to boast, for they can be cut off. God is able to graft the natural branches in again. Paul says all Israel will be saved and ends with praise.
events.detail: Verse 13 says Paul now speaks to Gentiles. Verse 17 gives their place: wild olive branches grafted in among the others. They share the root; they did not grow it. Verse 18 forbids boasting over the broken branches and gives the reason. The root holds them up, and they do not hold up the root. Verse 20 says they stand only by faith and should fear. Verse 23 adds that God can graft the others in again.

No one should think too highly of himself. They are one body with many members and different gifts. Paul lists the gifts and then short commands about love. Bless those who persecute you. The other person’s answer is not in that part. Verse 19 names what is given up: revenge belongs to God. Verse 20 names what remains to do: give an enemy food and drink.

ancientRoads.title: Appian Way
ancientRoads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Egnatia
ancientRoads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

ancientRoads.title: Via Sebaste
ancientRoads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
ancientRoads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Cilician Gates pass
ancientRoads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
ancientRoads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem. The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.

regions.name: Judea · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
regions.detail: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

regions.name: Syria · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
regions.detail: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Cilicia · approximate
regions.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
regions.detail: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

regions.name: Cyprus · Roman province
regions.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
regions.detail: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
regions.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

regions.name: Galatia · Roman province
regions.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
regions.detail: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

regions.name: Asia · Roman province
regions.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
regions.detail: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

regions.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
regions.detail: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

regions.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
regions.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
regions.detail: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

regions.name: Macedonia · Roman province
regions.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
regions.detail: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

regions.name: Achaia · Roman province
regions.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
regions.detail: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

regions.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
regions.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
regions.detail: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

regions.name: Italy
regions.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
regions.detail: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

guides.title: Romans: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Abraham's trust comes before the sign
steps.text: Verse 9 asks whether the blessing is only for the circumcised. Verse 10 answers with the order of events in Abraham’s life. He was counted righteous first and circumcised later. Verse 11 then calls circumcision a sign and seal of the faith he already had. That order makes him father of two groups. He is father of all who believe without circumcision (verse 11). He is also father of the circumcised who walk in that faith (verse 12).

steps.title: The Spirit helps within weakness rather than removing every groan
steps.text: Verses 22–23 describe two groans: creation’s and the believers’. Both wait for something not yet seen (verses 24–25). Verse 26 adds a third groan, and it is the Spirit’s. The weakness it names is exact: we do not know how to pray. The Spirit pleads for us with groans that cannot be spoken. Verse 27 says God, who searches hearts, knows the Spirit’s mind.

steps.title: The added branches must not boast against their supporting root
steps.text: Verse 13 says Paul now speaks to Gentiles. Verse 17 gives their place: wild olive branches grafted in among the others. They share the root; they did not grow it. Verse 18 forbids boasting over the broken branches and gives the reason. The root holds them up, and they do not hold up the root. Verse 20 says they stand only by faith and should fear. Verse 23 adds that God can graft the others in again.

steps.title: Welcome refuses to turn disputed practices into judgment of another servant
steps.text: Two groups disagree about food and days (verses 2 and 5). Verses 3–4 tell each to stop despising or judging the other. Verse 14 gives Paul’s own view: no food is unclean in itself. He does not use that view to settle the matter. Verse 15 says food must not destroy one for whom Christ died. Verse 19 states the aim that replaces winning: peace and building one another up. Verse 20 names the other course: tearing down God’s work for food.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul opens a letter to the believers in Rome. He calls himself an apostle set apart for God’s good news about his Son. He thanks God that their faith is known in all the world. He has often planned to visit and has been prevented. He says he is not ashamed of the good news. It is God’s power to save the Jew first and also the Greek. God’s wrath, he says, falls on those who trade his glory for images. God gives them up to their desires, and Paul lists the wrongs that follow.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul turns to a person who judges others. He says the judge does the same things and will not escape God’s judgment. God’s kindness is meant to lead to repentance. God will repay each one according to works, Jew first and also Greek. There is no partiality with God. Gentiles without the law sometimes do what the law requires. Paul then questions a Jewish teacher of the law who breaks it. He says true circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul asks what advantage the Jew has and answers that it is great. They were entrusted with God’s words. Still he says Jews and Greeks are all under sin. He quotes a chain of Scriptures: no one is righteous. The law stops every mouth and gives knowledge of sin. Now God’s righteousness comes apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ. All have sinned, and all are justified freely by grace. Boasting is shut out, and faith upholds the law.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul takes Abraham as his example. Scripture says Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. A worker’s pay is owed, but this was counted as a gift. David also calls blessed the one whose sin the Lord does not count. Paul asks when Abraham was counted righteous. It was before he was circumcised. The promise came through faith, so it holds for all his offspring. Abraham trusted God for a son when he was about a hundred years old.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says those justified by faith have peace with God. They rejoice in hope and even in sufferings. Suffering produces perseverance, character, and hope. Christ died for the ungodly while they were still weak. Those once enemies are reconciled through his death. Paul then compares Adam and Christ. Through one man sin and death came to all. Through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul asks if believers should keep sinning so that grace may grow. He answers that it must never be. Those baptized into Christ were baptized into his death. The old self was crucified with him, and the dead are freed from sin. They are to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God. Paul asks again if freedom from law permits sin. He says a person is a servant of what he obeys. The wages of sin is death, but God’s free gift is eternal life.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says the law binds a person only while he lives. A wife is free to marry again when her husband dies. So believers died to the law through Christ’s body and belong to another. Paul asks if the law is sin and denies it. He would not have known coveting without the command not to covet. Sin used the command and brought death. He describes wanting the good and doing the evil he hates. He cries out for rescue and thanks God through Jesus Christ.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. God sent his Son to do what the law could not. Those led by God’s Spirit are God’s children and call him Abba, Father. They are heirs with Christ if they suffer with him. Creation groans and waits to be set free from decay. Believers groan too and wait in hope. The Spirit helps them pray. Paul says nothing can separate them from God’s love in Christ.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says he has great sorrow for his own people, the Israelites. He lists their gifts, and says Christ came from them by descent. He says God’s word has not failed. Not all descended from Israel are Israel, as Isaac and Jacob show. God told Moses he has mercy on whom he will. Paul answers an objector with the potter and the clay. He quotes Hosea and Isaiah on a people called and a remnant saved. Israel pursued righteousness by works and stumbled over the stone.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says his prayer for Israel is that they be saved. They have zeal for God but not according to knowledge. He says Christ is the fulfillment of the law for everyone who believes. The word is near, in the mouth and in the heart. Whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised him will be saved. There is no distinction between Jew and Greek. Paul asks how people can call on one they have not heard. He quotes Isaiah: not all obeyed, yet God held out his hands all day.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul asks if God has rejected his people and says no. He is an Israelite himself, and a remnant remains as in Elijah’s day. Israel’s stumble has brought salvation to the Gentiles. Paul compares Israel to an olive tree. Some branches were broken off, and wild branches were grafted in. He warns the wild branches not to boast, for they can be cut off. God is able to graft the natural branches in again. Paul says all Israel will be saved and ends with praise.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul urges the believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice. They are not to be shaped by this world but changed by a renewed mind. No one should think too highly of himself. They are one body with many members and different gifts. Paul lists the gifts and then short commands about love. Bless those who persecute you. Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. Leave revenge to God, feed a hungry enemy, and overcome evil with good.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul tells every person to be subject to the governing authorities. He says they are appointed by God and carry the sword against wrongdoing. Believers should pay taxes, customs, respect, and honor where owed. They should owe nothing except love for one another. Love of neighbor sums up the commands against adultery, murder, theft, and coveting. Paul says the night is nearly over and the day is near. They should put away deeds of darkness. They should put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul tells the believers to accept one who is weak in faith. One eats everything, and another eats only vegetables. One honors a certain day, and another treats all days alike. Each does it for the Lord and will answer to God. So they must stop judging one another. Paul says nothing is unclean in itself. Yet they must not grieve a brother by what they eat. God’s kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul says the strong should bear the weaknesses of the weak. Christ did not please himself. Paul tells them to accept one another as Christ accepted them. He quotes four Scriptures about Gentiles praising God. He explains that he has taught from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. He plans to visit Rome on his way to Spain. First he will carry a gift from Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem’s poor. He asks them to pray for his safety in Judea.

chapterMaps.narrative: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the assembly at Cenchreae. He asks the Romans to receive her and help her. He greets Prisca and Aquila, who risked their necks for him. He greets many others by name, among them Mary, Andronicus, Junia, and Rufus. He warns against those who cause divisions. Timothy and others send greetings. Tertius, who wrote the letter down, adds his own. The letter ends with a blessing.
